column3: The Hebrew does not repeat Jonathan’s name in the final clause; BSB names him.
The Hebrew describes Saul as sitting and calls those with him “the people”; BSB uses “staying” and “troops”.
The Hebrew calls them “the people”, not troops, and introduces Ahijah with “and”, not an explicit “including”.
The Hebrew calls the cliffs rock teeth and uses plural “passes”; BSB has “cliffs” and singular “the pass”.
The Hebrew repeats the image of the tooth for the first cliff.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew repeats “your heart” in the final phrase; BSB adds the idiom “heart and soul”.
The Hebrew says “behold”; BSB renders the opening as “Very well”.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew has singular “our hand”; BSB uses plural “our hands” and rearranges the sign clause into the stated reason for going up.
The Hebrew explicitly repeats “the Philistines” as speakers; BSB uses a relative pronoun.
The Hebrew says to come up after him and describes making them know something; BSB says “Follow me” and “teach you a lesson”.
The Hebrew uses unnamed “they” for those falling; BSB identifies them as Philistines.
The Hebrew retains the agricultural images of a furrow, yoke, and field; BSB gives the area as half an acre.
The Hebrew first says there was trembling without naming the Philistines, and repeatedly uses the trembling root; BSB names them and varies terror, trembling, and panic.
The Hebrew calls the dissolving group “the multitude”; BSB calls them troops.
The Hebrew explicitly introduces “behold” when they find the two absent; BSB gives this as their seeing.
The Hebrew explicitly repeats “the ark of God”; BSB uses “it”.
The Hebrew repeats the going root in describing the increasing commotion; BSB condenses this.
The Hebrew says each man’s sword was against his neighbor, rather than explicitly making wielding it a further action. It does not name the Philistines again.
The Hebrew explicitly measures the former time with “yesterday and the day before” and uses singular “the camp”; BSB has “previously” and plural “camps”.
The Hebrew says they followed closely after the fleeing people in battle; BSB instead explicitly says they joined Saul and Jonathan.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew explicitly repeats bread for eating and tasting and calls the group the people; BSB says food and troops.
The Hebrew metonymically says “all the land”; BSB says “all the troops”.
The Hebrew twice explicitly names the people; BSB uses pronouns for them.
The Hebrew says his hand was returned to his mouth; BSB says he put it there.
The Hebrew says a man from the people answered and spoke; BSB calls him a soldier and says he told him.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew does not explicitly say “better”; the comparison and conditional eating lead into the question about the blow.
